opus-5.5.text:
I think of them as complementary rather than competing explanations. For a long time the dominant story was that scaling pretraining compute, meaning more parameters and more tokens, would gradually give you better reasoning as a byproduct. That did happen to a degree. Larger models trained on internet text pick up a surprising amount of latent reasoning ability, because the web contains a lot of worked math, code, and argumentation.

What we've seen more recently is that the bottleneck isn't only raw scale. It's also the kind of data the model learns from and the training signal you give it. Internet text mostly shows you final answers, or polished reasoning written after the fact. It doesn't show you the messy process: trying an approach, noticing it fails, backtracking. When you train models on reasoning traces, especially traces generated and filtered through reinforcement learning against verifiable outcomes like whether code passes tests or a proof checks, you get much better performance per unit of compute on those tasks.

The way I'd frame the relationship is that scale gives you the substrate. A bigger, better-pretrained base model has richer representations, so it's a better starting point for reasoning-focused training, and it can produce higher-quality reasoning traces of its own. Reasoning data and RL then elicit and sharpen that capability. There's a feedback loop: better models generate better synthetic reasoning data, which trains better models. That loop is part of why progress on math and coding benchmarks has been so fast.

There's also a compute angle people sometimes miss. Reasoning-style training shifts some compute from pretraining to post-training and to inference. Letting a model think longer at test time is itself a form of scaling. So I wouldn't say data has replaced scaling. Scaling has become multidimensional. You can scale pretraining, RL on reasoning tasks, and inference-time compute, and the interesting empirical question is how to allocate across them.

One caveat is that much of this works best in domains with cheap, reliable verification: math, programming, some science problems. How well it generalizes to fuzzier domains, where it's hard to check whether the reasoning was good, is still fairly open. My guess is that progress there will be slower and lean more on scale and transfer than on clean reward signals. But the overall picture is that data quality and compute are multiplicative. You need both, and gains in one make the other more valuable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a bigger, better-pretrained base model can produce higher-quality reasoning traces, and describes using reasoning traces in reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about this is that reasoning data and scaling aren't really substitutes for each other—they're complements, and the interesting question is about the shape of that complementarity.

For a long time, the story in AI was pretty simple: you scale up compute, you scale up parameters, you scale up the pretraining data, and you get predictable improvements across a broad range of capabilities. And that story is still basically true. But what we've seen over the past couple of years with the reasoning models—the o1-style, R1-style models—is that there's a second axis you can push on, which is training on data that specifically elicits long chains of thought, verification, backtracking, that kind of thing. And that data is often generated by the models themselves through reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards, so it's not like you're going out and scraping it from the internet.

What's striking to me is how little of that data you seem to need, at least initially, to unlock quite a lot. There were results where a few thousand carefully chosen reasoning traces were enough to get a base model to behave much more like a reasoning model. So the reasoning data looks like it's doing something more like unlocking or eliciting a capability that's already latent in the base model, rather than teaching it from scratch.

And that's where scaling comes back in. The size of the latent capability—how much there is to elicit—seems to depend heavily on how good the base model is, which is a function of pretraining scale. If you take a small model and give it the same reasoning data, you get much less out of it. So in a sense, scaling sets the ceiling, and reasoning data and RL determine how close you get to that ceiling, at least in the regime we've been in.

Now, I'd add a caveat, which is that I don't think this stays a cheap, data-light story forever. Once you've picked the low-hanging fruit of elicitation, further gains in reasoning seem to require scaling up the RL phase itself—more environments, more rollouts, more compute spent on generating and filtering those reasoning traces. And when you look at what the labs are actually doing, the compute going into post-training and RL is growing really fast, in some cases approaching what goes into pretraining. So I'd expect reasoning data to become its own scaling story, with its own scaling laws, rather than remaining this small, clever intervention on top of a big pretrained model.

So, if I had to summarize: scaling gives you the raw substrate, reasoning data tells the model how to use it, and increasingly the production of that reasoning data is itself becoming one of the main things we scale.

r001.rationale: The response says models can generate reasoning data through reinforcement learning, but does not state that larger models generate higher-quality reasoning traces.

astra-6.text:
I think reasoning data and model scaling are complementary. Scaling gives you a model that can absorb more structure from its training data, but the kind of data you train on matters a great deal. If you want a model to solve problems that require several steps, examples of those steps can provide a richer learning signal than just the final answer.

There’s also a potentially important feedback loop. Once a model is capable enough to solve some difficult problems, you can have it generate solutions, check which ones work, and use those to train a better model. That’s particularly promising in domains like mathematics and programming, where you can often verify an answer relatively cheaply even when finding it is difficult.

But generating more reasoning text isn’t automatically useful. You need some way of selecting for correctness and for approaches that generalize. Otherwise, you might simply reinforce mistakes or produce lots of repetitive examples.

So I wouldn’t view reasoning data as a substitute for scaling. It can make training compute more productive, while larger, more capable models can help produce better reasoning data. And then there’s a separate dimension of scaling: letting the model spend more compute at inference time, exploring and checking possible solutions. Training on good reasoning data can help it use that additional compute effectively.

r001.rationale: The response says larger, more capable models can help produce better reasoning data for training, but it does not specify that this data is used in reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two complementary things going on. One is that scaling models gives you a stronger starting point: a model that has learned more about the world and has more capabilities that you can draw on. The other is that reasoning data can teach the model how to use those capabilities—how to break a problem down, explore possible solutions, and check its work.

And those interact. A larger model might be better able to learn from a sophisticated reasoning trace, while better reasoning data might let a smaller model achieve performance that would otherwise require substantially more scale. So I wouldn’t think of reasoning data as simply replacing scaling. It changes what you get out of a given amount of scale.

There’s also a feedback loop if models can generate useful reasoning data themselves. You can have a model attempt a problem, verify which answers are correct, and train on successful solutions. That potentially lets you improve reasoning without relying entirely on humans to write out examples. But how far that takes you depends on whether you can reliably check the answers, whether the generated data adds something new, and whether those improvements generalize beyond the problems you’re training on.

r001.rationale: The response says models can generate and train on successful solutions, but does not state that larger models generate higher-quality reasoning traces for reinforcement learning.
